# War in the Middle East

*This page provides background and the most recent updates on the conflict in the Middle East involving the United States, Israel, Iran, and Lebanon.*

The relationship between the United States and Iran has been difficult for many decades. The two countries have often disagreed over power and resources.  
     In the 1950s, a major disagreement began over oil. Iran’s leader at that time wanted Iran to have full control over its own oil. The US helped remove the leader, and gave the Shah (the country’s king) full power. The Shah ruled harshly. And because the U.S. helped keep the Shah in power, many Iranians began to distrust the US.  
     In 1979, the people of Iran began protesting the Shah. The huge protests turned into a revolution. The Shah was forced to leave the country. A new group of leaders took over and turned Iran into a country with a religious Islamic government. Protesters took control of the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 people hostage for over a year. This created a mistrust between the two nations that still exists today.

# US-Iran escalation prompts debate in Iran over preemptive strikes

![Maryam Sinaiee](https://i.iranintl.com/images/rdk9umy0/production/45ee979fa99e8002d6eaa062959bc17d6e4fd2ff-1520x2026.jpg?rect=0,253,1520,1520&w=96&h=96&q=58&fit=max&sat=-100&auto=format)

[Maryam Sinaiee](https://www.iranintl.com/en/author/maryam-sinaiee)

Iran International

Smoke rises following a US strike on Iran’s Larak Island on August 30, 2026.



Calls for preemptive strikes on US forces are growing in Iran after renewed US attacks, intensifying debate over whether Tehran should shift away from a mainly retaliatory strategy.

The latest cycle began with a US strike on Revolutionary Guards targets on Larak Island in Hormozgan province Sunday night, after a period in which Washington had increasingly emphasized economic pressure, a naval blockade and additional sanctions on Iran.

Iranian authorities initially reported two deaths, but the toll later rose to three after one of the wounded died in hospital, according to the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency.

US Central Command said the Larak strike targeted an “imminent threat,” alleging Revolutionary Guards forces were preparing to launch rockets carrying sea mines toward the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran rejected that account.

Grushko stated that Moscow will only return to the deal if the West eases sanctions on Russian agricultural exports. The diplomat maintained that Russia backed out of the original agreement because Western promises to allow Russian food, fertilizer, and financial payments into global markets were never fulfilled.

# The Instrument

### Part II: What They Built During the Ceasefire

Series: The Instrument. How the West’s favourite economic weapon changed hands.

Between October 2025 and June 2026, the American Bureau of Industry and Security did not add a single company to the Entity List.

That is the longest such gap since 2008. Between 2018 and 2024 the average interval between additions was about thirty-five days. For eight months, the most active instrument of American technology policy sat completely still.

It looked like peace. It was a construction period.

### The trade, restated

The Busan meeting on 30 October 2025 produced a package, and the export control portion of it was a straight swap.

Washington suspended the Affiliates Rule for one year, to 9 November 2026. Beijing suspended the six October announcements, including the extraterritorial rare earth rule, to 10 November 2026. Beijing also returned gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite to its standard licensing framework and agreed to issue general licences for American end users. Washington halved the fentanyl linked tariff, extended tariff exclusions, and suspended the measures arising from its investigation into China’s maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors.

One year after China imposed export controls on seven heavy rare earths and magnets, analysts at CSIS warn the move exposed a critical US vulnerability: American electronics, EVs, wind turbines, and defense systems still depend on materials China controls the global supply of. Washington has poured billions into a response — but the mines and refineries take years.

The chemistry matters here: rare earths aren't rare — they're incredibly hard to separate. Refining them requires hundreds of chemical steps, and China built the world's only large-scale refining infrastructure decades ago. That's why a single country controls over 90% of processed supply, turning a rock problem into a leverage problem.

The controversy: nations are now weaponizing basic science. Export restrictions, tariffs, and counter-restrictions have turned periodic elements into chips in a geopolitical poker game.
